units.translation: Composition and rhythms. The strophic composition of this stasimon, according to the tradition, is as follows: Str. ⟦1⟧ Antistr. ⟦2⟧; each in two parts, consisting of a main part and a refrain that is identical in wording both times; Str. ⟦3⟧, with a refrain that one may call ⟦4⟧, in similar but not identical rhythms to that of ⟦5⟧, and with different words; Ant. ⟦6⟧; Str. ⟦7⟧, with the refrain ⟦8⟧ repeated rhythmically but not in wording; Str. ⟦9⟧ Ant. ⟦10⟧, without refrain. At ⟦11⟧ the peculiarity is that y attaches itself to ⟦12⟧ with the closest syntactic connection, which has not prevented modern editors (since G C W Schneider) from appending an identical ephymnion, thus lacking syntactic connection, also to the antistrophe ⟦13⟧; one repeats this at Str. Ant. ⟦14⟧, where at least the construction suffers no harm, though the sense certainly does, and so one obtains the regular scheme of ⟦15⟧. Correspondingly, it has been done in the last two stasima of the Choephori, where the tradition offers a similar artificial interweaving as here: ⟦16⟧. ⟦17⟧. and ⟦18⟧, as here ⟦19⟧. I do not understand how one can thus devastate the sense for the sake of a purely external scheme. Far less harsh, but in my opinion equally false, is the formerly popular transposition of y' after ⟦20⟧, by which likewise the regular scheme ⟦21⟧ is obtained; see on Antistr. ⟦22⟧. In the scholia (on 341) is found the name fitting the transmitted form ⟦23⟧ (that which is sung between two strophes). A. has two kinds of ephymnia, identical in wording and only rhythmically identical; the former kind appears ⟦24⟧. 139. 159 (1 verse). ⟦25⟧. 972 (likewise); more extensive ⟦26⟧; on the other hand the latter ⟦27⟧, with rhythmic identity throughout the whole stasimon except for the epode, and ⟦28⟧ likewise except for the last strophic pair, with the same rhythms as in the Agam.; in addition ⟦29⟧ Str. Ant. ⟦30⟧ and the same also ⟦31⟧ have this character. The rhythms show the same progression from majestic trochees to pathetic iambs as so often in A., see on ⟦32⟧. With the trochees are combined here as elsewhere dactyls, and again in pentapodies, ⟦33⟧ (p. 78). 591 f. (p. 143); yet this is not yet the case in the first strophe, but in the second and third to such a strong degree that the dactyls far predominate and there is only one trochaic colon in each. In these strophes, which one will therefore call ⟦34⟧, there occur besides the pentapodies other dactylic verses, see below on Str. ⟦35⟧. Finally, also in the iambic strophe ⟦36⟧ the close is again a dactylic pentapody with trochaic dimeter, as in the iambic ⟦37⟧. But the refrain in ⟦38⟧ and the strophe serving as refrain ⟦39⟧ have, besides trochees, whose dipody for the most part shows the first arsis resolved and the last thesis suppressed (thus ∪ ∪ ∪ —), in all appearance also the Pherecratean, thus a ⟦40⟧ from ⟦41⟧, so at the end ⟦42⟧ (as ⟦43⟧ at the end and likewise in the following strophes; again 681 ff. at the end and likewise in Str. ⟦44⟧) and according to the tradition also in the middle of the refrain of ⟦45⟧, see below; accordingly it is to be investigated whether the same is also to be recognized at the beginning of ⟦46⟧. Characteristic for the ⟦47⟧ are the measures ∪ ∪ ∪ — (almost always with diaeresis after each measure); everything else is found also used elsewhere, in that at least from Antistr. ⟦48⟧ onward, outside the refrains, self-conscious majesty presents itself in the song. Strophe ⟦49⟧. The rhythms are according to the tradition unclear precisely at the beginning, but Weil has made something very pleasing out of it, though not without alteration: (Antistr.) ⟦50⟧ | (- -,-∪「,「「) ⟦51⟧ (⟦52⟧ likewise) ⟦53⟧ )-)」, ں۔۔۔, -ur, 「「), and accordingly Str.: ⟦54⟧ | ⟦55⟧, ⟦56⟧ (⟦57⟧(⟦58⟧) transmitted) ⟦59⟧. The ⟦60⟧ of the form ⟦61⟧ and again ⟦62⟧ – ⟦63⟧, correspondingly at the close of the cola, make themselves most magnificent, whereas if one divides and measures thus (Rossbach-Westphal): ⟦64⟧, ⟦65⟧ | ⟦66⟧, one obtains in the first verse a mixture of trochees and dactyls (or Pherecratean), and as the second the ⟦67⟧ وساسا ⟦68⟧ which would be measured as - c, rit, with the form for -- nowhere attested. ⟦69⟧ and ⟦70⟧ differ little, and the meaning "blind" is present for ⟦71⟧ at least in Sophocles, ⟦72⟧ ⟦73⟧, 1639 ⟦74⟧ ("dark" also A., ⟦75⟧ etc.). The connection is as below 387 ⟦76⟧, and if ⟦77⟧ corresponds even better to ⟦78⟧ than ⟦79⟧, it may have come in as the more familiar word for "blind". Lengthenings as in ⟦80⟧ are found in A. also the following (J. Rumpel Progr. Insterburg [I. II] 1865. 66): ⟦81⟧ ⟦82⟧ (⟦83⟧ Ddf.), ⟦84⟧ ⟦85⟧, ⟦86⟧ ⟦87⟧, ⟦88⟧ ⟦89⟧, ⟦90⟧ ⟦91⟧, ⟦92⟧ (Ddf. ⟦93⟧) ⟦94⟧, ⟦95⟧ ⟦96⟧. Thus there seem to be preponderant reasons for the change. The imperfect ⟦97⟧ corresponds to the rule according to which of persons still living the imperfect and not the aorist is used, Homer Ζ 206 ⟦98⟧, against ⟦99⟧ 196. 199 (not very different 154 ⟦100⟧ and 155 ⟦101⟧, where the narrative lingers, as it were "has (had) borne"), likewise ⟦102⟧ 118 ⟦103⟧, ⟦104⟧ (whom Telemachus holds for dead), ⟦105⟧ (for Odysseus I have been nothing). For the sense of ⟦106⟧ Paley rightly compares 175. 340; see also on 302. –
